summary: On the ISS, an astronaut who feels unwell can talk to a doctor within seconds. On Mars, a reply can take 44 minutes, and during solar conjunction it may not come at all. Today’s health tools can tell a crew that a reading looks wrong. They can’t tell them who should do something about it. We built FARSIDE to answer that. It reads the crew’s vital signs and cabin air, compares them with medical guidelines and with each person’s own normal, and then looks at how far away Earth is right now. If help from the ground is only minutes away, Earth makes the call. If it isn’t, the crew medic gets clear instructions straight away. A report still goes back to Earth, with a countdown showing when the reply should arrive. The readings don’t change. Only the distance does, and so does the decision.
details:
We started with a simple question: if an astronaut on Mars gets a worrying reading, who decides what happens next? Every health monitor we found stops at “this number is abnormal”. When the doctor is 20 minutes away one way, that isn’t enough.

FARSIDE works in four steps.

First, it takes readings. Our physical station runs a 20-second reaction and balance test and measures CO2 in the cabin. We built the remaining health channels as an ESP32 simulation in Wokwi, and the app clearly labels those values as simulated.

Second, it scores each reading. We check every value against the NEWS2 early warning score, NASA standards and that crew member’s own baseline. A number that is normal for one person can be a warning sign for someone else.

Third, it decides who acts. We combine how serious the finding is with how long Earth would take to answer. If the round trip is under 10 minutes, Earth decides. If it is longer, or there’s no link at all, the crew acts. We picked the 10-minute line ourselves, based on NASA’s guidance on when crews are expected to work independently.

Fourth, it explains the result. An AI model turns the decision into plain language the crew can act on right away. We were careful here: a transparent rules engine makes every decision, and the AI only explains it. It never changes a tier. That keeps each decision checkable, which matters when it’s someone’s health.

Here’s an example. An oxygen saturation of 91 percent on the ISS means “send it to Earth, a flight surgeon will answer in seconds”. The same reading on Mars means “the crew medic acts now”.

We wanted the data to be real wherever we could. Four crew baselines come from actual Inspiration4 pre-flight blood tests in NASA’s Open Science Data Repository. Our stress model, trained on the WESAD dataset, reached 91.6 percent accuracy when tested on people it had never seen. Even so, we only use it as a flag. Solar particle events come from NASA DONKI, and the delay figures come from NASA and AIAA research.

The app shows who needs to act, what to do now and how long until Earth replies. A 3D body view links each part of the astronaut to the test that checks it.

We built it with React, TypeScript, Three.js, FastAPI, Python, Arduino, ESP32 on Wokwi, scikit-learn, LightGBM and the Claude API.

Next, we’d like to request access to NASA astronaut health records and train the on-board model on them. We also want to compare every on-board assessment with the diagnosis Earth sends back, so the system can learn from its mistakes. On a real mission it would run on hardware the crew wears, not in the cloud.
